q: What is the primary objective of the NSTP law (RA 9163)?
options: To replace all college subjects with military training
To promote the role of the youth in nation-building
To register all students as voters
To create the National Youth Commission
explanation: NSTP encourages the youth to become civic or military leaders and volunteers. The National Youth Commission came from RA 8044.

q: What is the Civic Welfare Training Service (CWTS)?
options: The component that prepares the youth for national defense
The component that trains students to teach reading, writing, and numeracy
The component for activities with social impact on the health, education, environment, entrepreneurship, safety, recreation, and morals of the citizenry
The office that registers voters
explanation: CWTS covers broad community welfare activities. Teaching literacy and numeracy is LTS, and defense is ROTC.

q: What is the Literacy Training Service (LTS)?
options: The component that trains students to teach literacy and numeracy skills to school children, out-of-school youth, and others in need
The component that trains students in military drills
The program that started political development
The component for environment and entrepreneurship projects
explanation: LTS specializes in education, training students as teachers of literacy and numeracy.

q: What is the primary objective of the Military Training Service, also known as ROTC?
options: To teach numeracy to out-of-school youth
To run barangay elections
To promote ecological balance
To prepare the youth for national defense
explanation: ROTC prepares the youth for national defense. Under the NSTP law it became one of the three equal components.

q: What is political development?
options: The constant progress or social mobility of every individual
The active participation and involvement of all individuals in governmental activities and public affairs
The harmonious relationship of people from different cultures and religions
The protection of the country's territory
explanation: Political development is about taking part in government and public affairs. Social mobility describes economic development.

q: What is socio-cultural development?
options: The harmonious relationship of individuals from different social groups, cultures, and religions, and the preservation of cultural virtues and values
The presence of adequate economic resources
Participation in elections
Cordial relations with neighboring countries
explanation: Socio-cultural development is about getting along across groups and keeping the values needed for moral development.

q: What is cultural cohesiveness?
options: Agreement on a national vision and on what is right and wrong
Peace and harmony between the government and the people
People sharing the values and beliefs handed down by their forebears, with a strong attachment to the national community despite differences
A strong economy owned by the people
explanation: Cultural cohesiveness is shared values and beliefs. Agreement on goals, right and wrong, and a national vision is moral consensus.

q: What is moral consensus?
options: Sharing the same language and religion
People inspired by patriotism actively pursue the nation's goals and agree on where the nation is going, on right and wrong, and on a national vision
Protecting the environment for sustainable development
Keeping rebels out of the territory
explanation: Moral consensus is agreement on goals, morals, and vision. Shared values and beliefs from forebears is cultural cohesiveness.

q: What is territorial integrity?
options: Cordial relations with other countries
An environment that supports sustainable development
Respect for civil and human rights
The country's territory is intact and under the effective control of the government
explanation: Territorial integrity means the territory is whole, protected from illegal intrusions, and no rebel or belligerent group controls any part of it.

q: What is economic solidarity?
options: A strong economy that supports national endeavors and draws strength from people who have a stake in it through participation or ownership
Equal pay for every worker
Trade agreements with neighboring countries
The constant social mobility of every individual
explanation: Economic solidarity means the people control their own livelihoods and economic democracy prevails. Social mobility is part of economic development.

q: What is an election, as defined in the lesson?
options: A survey of public opinion
A meeting of local officials
The means by which the people choose their officials for definite and fixed periods
The process of capturing a voter's fingerprints
explanation: Elections choose officials for fixed terms. Capturing fingerprints is validation of registration.

q: What is voter registration?
options: Voting on election day
Accomplishing and filing a sworn application for registration by a qualified voter
Transferring to a new residence
Running for public office
explanation: Registration is filing a sworn application. It must be done before a person can take part in electoral activities.

q: When was RA 9163, the NSTP law, signed into law?
options: January 23, 2002
June 7, 2002
January 23, 1995
March 1993
explanation: RA 9163 was signed on January 23, 2002. RA 8044, the Youth in Nation-Building Act, was enacted in 1995.

q: Under RA 8044, what age range counts as the Filipino youth?
explanation: The Youth in Nation-Building Act defines the youth as those aged 15 to 30.

q: Which laws did RA 9163 amend?
options: RA 8044 and RA 9165
The 1987 Constitution and RA 8044
PD 1706 and the Local Government Code
RA 7077 and PD 1706
explanation: The full title says the NSTP Act amends Republic Act No. 7077 and Presidential Decree No. 1706.

q: Which are the four special elections in the lesson?
options: National, local, barangay, and SK
Presidential, senatorial, local, and plebiscite
ARMM, SK, barangay, and recall
Plebiscite, referendum, initiative, and recall
explanation: National, local, barangay, ARMM, and SK are regular elections. Plebiscite, referendum, initiative, and recall are special elections.

q: When are barangay and SK elections held, according to the lesson?
options: Every second Monday of May, every 6 years
Every last Monday of October, every 3 years
Every first Monday of January, every 2 years
Every March, every 3 years
explanation: Barangay and SK elections are on the last Monday of October, every 3 years. National and local elections are on the second Monday of May.

q: What are the residency requirements for voter registration?
options: At least 1 year in the Philippines and at least 6 months in the city or municipality immediately before the election
At least 6 months in the Philippines and 1 year in the city
At least 2 years in the barangay
There is no residency requirement
explanation: A voter must have lived in the Philippines for at least 1 year and in the city or municipality for at least 6 months before the election.

q: Which order shows how the program developed?
options: NSTP, then E-ROTC, then ROTC
E-ROTC, then ROTC, then NSTP
ROTC, then E-ROTC, then NSTP
NSTP, then ROTC, then E-ROTC
explanation: ROTC specialized in military training, E-ROTC offered three options but was limited, and NSTP gave all three components equal implementation.

q: Which law came first?
options: RA 9163, the NSTP Act (2002)
Both were signed the same year
Neither has a known date
RA 8044, the Youth in Nation-Building Act (1995)
explanation: RA 8044 was enacted in 1995, seven years before RA 9163 was signed in 2002.

q: What is the order of steps to transfer your voter registration?
options: Apply with the Election Officer of your new residence for the transfer of your records, then accomplish six application forms
Vote first, then apply for transfer
Accomplish one form at the old residence, then wait for a recall
Register as a new voter at the COMELEC main office, then cancel the old record yourself
explanation: The lesson's two steps are to apply with the Election Officer of the new residence and to accomplish six application forms.

q: What is the right order for a new voter?
options: Vote, then register, then meet the requirements
Meet the requirements, register at the COMELEC office, have fingerprints captured for validation, then vote in the election
Have fingerprints captured, turn 18, then register
Transfer registration, then meet the requirements
explanation: Only a qualified person can file the sworn application; validation captures fingerprints; then the voter can choose leaders on election day.

q: Which pairing of an NSTP component and its focus is mismatched?
options: CWTS: community welfare activities
LTS: teaching literacy and numeracy
ROTC: national defense
LTS: preparing the youth for military service
explanation: Preparing for national defense is ROTC. LTS trains students to teach literacy and numeracy.

q: Which is NOT one of the seven elements of national security?
options: Ecological balance
Economic solidarity
Military superiority
External peace
explanation: The seven elements are cultural cohesiveness, moral consensus, territorial integrity, ecological balance, socio-political stability, economic solidarity, and external peace.

q: Which is NOT a requirement for voter registration?
options: Being a college graduate
Being a Filipino citizen
Being at least 18 years old
Not being disqualified by law
explanation: Education is not a requirement. The requirements are citizenship, age 18 or older, residency, and not being disqualified.

q: Which pairing of an element of national security and its meaning is mismatched?
options: External peace: cordial relations with neighboring countries
Socio-political stability: peace inside the country and cooperation between government and people
Ecological balance: an environment that supports sustainable development
Cultural cohesiveness: agreement on a national vision and on right and wrong
explanation: Agreement on a national vision and on right and wrong is moral consensus. Cultural cohesiveness is shared values and beliefs from forebears.

q: Which statement about election terms in the lesson is NOT true?
options: The President and Vice-President are elected every 6 years
Senators and Representatives are elected every 6 years, like the President
National and local elections are held every second Monday of May
Provincial, city, and municipal officials are elected every 3 years
explanation: The lesson lists Senators and Representatives with the every-3-year elections. Only the President and Vice-President are every 6 years.

q: A group of students teaches out-of-school youth in their barangay how to read and do basic arithmetic. Which NSTP component fits this?
options: Literacy Training Service (LTS)
Civic Welfare Training Service (CWTS)
Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC)
Voters' Education
explanation: Teaching literacy and numeracy to out-of-school youth is exactly what LTS trains students for.

q: Voters in a province vote on whether to remove their governor before the end of the term. What kind of election is this?
options: A regular local election
A plebiscite
A recall
A referendum
explanation: Removing an elected official before the term ends is a recall, one of the special elections.

q: A 19-year-old Filipino moved to a new city 4 months before the election and wants to vote there. Under the lesson's rules, what is the problem?
options: She is too young to vote
She has not lived in the city for at least 6 months before the election
She must first finish NSTP
She must be a resident of the Philippines for 5 years
explanation: She meets the age and citizenship rules, but the city residency requirement is at least 6 months immediately before the election.
